handouts.contentText:
I think I have been trapped beneath the mountain for eighty-three years.

At least, that is the number I settled on. After a while the years stopped meaning much. I counted seasons for a time, then floods, then cave-ins. I watched tribes of troglodytes rise and destroy one another, gricks claim new hunting grounds, and stirges build nests in places that had once been safe to sleep. Adventurers came now and then as well. Most of them died. The fortunate ones found a way back to the surface.

I remained.

In the beginning I believed I would escape. I had survived worse places before, and there was always another face to borrow, another town to disappear into, another life waiting somewhere else. Then the orcs came and everything changed. The old routes became dangerous, the lower halls even worse, and I discovered that many of the creatures living beneath the mountain could not be deceived. Troglodytes saw through disguises, gricks cared nothing for appearances, and the things that haunted the deep places had no interest in lies, ambition, or conversation.

Eventually I stopped becoming other people, because there was no one left to become.

The years passed into decades. I survived by hiding in cracks in the stone and forgotten chambers, listening to the sounds of the mountain and learning which dangers to avoid. It should have been enough simply to stay alive, but after long enough survival becomes its own kind of loneliness.

Whenever travelers passed through, I found myself following them from the darkness. I would watch them sit around their fires, listen to them argue and laugh, and pretend for a few stolen moments that I belonged among them. Then they would leave.

Or die. Usually die.

When the Brotherhood entered the mountain, I watched them the same way. At first they seemed no different from all the others who had come before them: a druid who spoke to trees, a wizard who could never resist touching things best left alone, a priest who survived wounds that should have killed him, and a half-orc named Balok.

He was not the cleverest among them, and despite what he might have claimed, he was not the strongest either. What made him different was that he was simple in a way I had almost forgotten people could be. He protected his friends. He carried what needed carrying. When danger appeared, he stepped in front of it. If he was angry, everyone knew. If he was worried, they knew that too. He never hid what he was.

I realized, after a while, that I was watching him more than the others. Then I realized I was thinking about him even when he was gone. One day, when there was no one around to see, I borrowed his face. At first it was only practice. I knew his voice, the way he walked, the way he carried his shoulders, and the way his hand drifted toward his weapon whenever he was uncertain. I could become him perfectly, and I told myself that was all it was—a game to pass the time.

Then they challenged the dragon. I watched the battle from the darkness near the Black Lake. I saw Balok fight, and I saw him vanish beneath the water after the dragon fled. I waited for him to surface, but he never did. The others searched for him and called his name until, eventually, they stopped. They believed he was dead. So did I.

For a long time I stayed near the shore where the lake vanished into darkness. Then I found one of his belongings drifting in the water. Later I found another, and then another, scattered by a drowning man struggling to survive. I gathered them all, cleaned them, and kept them. I told myself I was preserving what he had left behind. The truth was simpler. I was not ready to let him go.

When the Brotherhood finally turned back toward the upper levels, I followed them. Not closely—just near enough that I could keep the glow from the priests spells in sight. If they left, I would still be there beneath the mountain, waiting through another decade, then another twenty years, hiding from troglodytes and orcs until I forgot what people sounded like. I did not want that.

Without thinking, I found myself wearing Balok's face again. Then I put on the clothing and gear I had recovered from the lake. The pieces fit well enough. When I looked down, I saw his hands. When I caught my reflection in still water, I saw his face. And somehow it felt more like mine than my own.

That was when I understood what had happened. Balok had survived. Of course he had survived. Balok always survived.

The chimney was the answer. I had known about it for years. One of the first routes I discovered after arriving here. An old dwarven shaft running between levels of the mountain. Dangerous. Narrow. Unpleasant, but possible. We could get back to the Brotherhood, so we climbed. The work was slow and filthy. Old soot coated the stone. More than once we nearly slipped. More than once we wondered whether we had the strength left to make it all the way down. Eventually the shaft widened. We emerged where we had hoped. In Glitterham, near what looked to be the lair of the Troglodites. Vaguely, we remembered it was there, and how we could escape. There was a door the wizard - Ezzilby? had found. It was open - we could use it.

They would want to know about the Troglodite lair - best to not leave an enemy behind if the Brotherhood intended to face the orcs above. I saw chests and tresure, perhaps more of the weapons needed for our quest. They would be happy to see I had survived and returned. If I hurried, I could catch them and rejoin the Brotherhood. I made it to the room where we fought the stirges, the room where Ezzilby accidentally froze Loneoak's tail when he was in his bear form. The memory still makes me smile. I can see Joric's light just fading out as they reach the top of the stairs. I can catch them if I run.

handouts.title: The Prisoners of the Stone Tooth [Balok]
handouts.summary:

The half-orc awoke alone in the Black Mire, battered nearly beyond recognition after the battle
handouts.contentText:
The tale of the Brotherhood of Regrowth did not end beneath the Black Lake.

While Loneoak, Ezzilby, and Joric struggled upward through Khundrukar, believing their companion lost beneath the dark waters, Balok still lived.

The half-orc awoke alone in the Black Mire, battered nearly beyond recognition after the battle with the black dragon. Swept through the dragon's escape tunnel and carried into the swamp, he survived only by stubbornness and a little luck. He found shelter in an abandoned dragon cult cave, where fever and exhaustion held him for several days.

He was not alone for long.

One night, voices carried through the rain outside the cave. A band of Blooded Hand orcs had come searching the abandoned camp, turning over old crates, kicking through ashes, and looking for anything the dragon cult might have left behind. Too weak to fight, Balok hid and listened.

The orcs spoke openly. Great Ulfe had sent them. They cursed the dead cultists, argued over missing orders and old symbols, and grumbled that their chief was chasing ghosts. Whatever the truth of it, even the Blooded Hand seemed uneasy about the strangers who had once occupied the cave.

Balok let them leave before he dared to move.

By the time he could stand without falling, only one thought remained.

Find the Brotherhood.

He made his way back toward the Stone Tooth and searched for the old orc tunnel the party had used to enter the mountain. What he found was a wall of broken stone. The passage had collapsed completely. Balok refused to believe it at first. He dug with his hands until his fingers bled. He shifted loose rocks one by one, searching for a gap large enough to squeeze through. He tried to pry larger stones free with broken branches and scraps of rusted iron scattered around the old entrance.

Hours passed. Exhaustion had already taken much from him. Every armful of stone left his muscles shaking. Every breath reminded him of black water filling his lungs. At last he accepted what the mountain had been trying to tell him from the beginning. The tunnel was completely collapsed.

He rested as best he could beneath the trees and turned his eyes toward the cliffs. There was one path left.

The old chimney.

The Brotherhood had found it before. They had studied it. Balok remembered the climb and remembered The Brotherhood deciding that party wouldn't survive the climb. Now, with the tunnel sealed and no sign of his friends, he had no better choice. The climb to the chimney mouth was slow work. The paths above the Black Mire were little more than game trails winding through old stone and stubborn brush. More than once he was forced to stop and catch his breath. More than once he wondered if the climb would simply claim him before he ever reached the entrance.

When he finally stood before it, smoke stains from ages past still marked the old stone. Cold air drifted up the shear cliffs of the mountain around him, pulling the wisps of smoke away on the winds. Somewhere beyond that narrow shaft lay Khundrukar. Somewhere beyond it were his friends.

Balok stood before the old chimney and studied the black opening below him. Behind him lay the swamp. Ahead of him lay the mountain. He tightened the straps on what gear remained and looked out over the early morning skies one last time........

There was no chance he could make that climb down the shaft of the chimney. Considering his injuries and lingering exhaustion convinced him that the climb would likely kill him. With no easy path available, he turned his attention to the main gate. In the early hours of the morning, he found the entrance guards bored and inattentive. Listening to their conversation, he learned enough about the tribe to bluff them into believing Great Ulfe wanted them elsewhere. The pair abandoned their post, and Balok quietly slipped inside.

Fortune stayed with him for a little while longer.

The longbow orcs watching through the murder holes had also grown careless. Balok reached the hidden southern guard post, where he silently killed an Orc Boss and one of the archers. From their bodies he gathered weapons, equipment, and a serviceable disguise. Dressed as one of the Blooded Hand's own leaders, he crossed the rope bridge and intimidated the guards into letting him pass.

Deeper inside the fortress he found the main sleeping cavern and made a troubling discovery. Two prisoners remained alive in the orcs' custody locked away in a crude cage. Balok considered freeing them, but without a safe route out he would only be leading them to their deaths. He left them where they were and continued searching for a way back to his friends.

His scouting paid off. In the kitchens he discovered the chimney route and confirmed that it could be used to enter or leave the Mountain Door. Still unwilling to risk the climb in his weakened state, he pressed onward.

The disguise began to fail in the supply chambers.

Finding a group of orcs working to barricade the old passage the Brotherhood had opened during their earlier expedition, Balok improvised another lie. He convinced them that the prisoners were escaping and slipped away while they rushed to investigate.

Unfortunately, the alarm did exactly what alarms are supposed to do.

The local Orc Boss woke the barracks, checked the prisoners, and discovered that nothing was wrong. Suspicious, he went looking for the orc who had raised the false alarm. At almost the same moment, Balok forgot one of the rules that had kept him alive all night.

He stopped checking doors.

He opened the entrance to the next guard room just as a fresh duty shift was preparing to relieve their companions. He quickly closed the door, but the damage was done. As he turned away, the suspicious Orc Boss rounded the corner and loudly demanded an explanation for the false alarm. The disguise was finished.

Balok ran.

He sprinted into the trapped corridor and triggered the ancient dwarven poison gas. Somehow he fought off the effects, but in his rush to escape he threw open another door and found Old Yarrack and his off-duty warriors settling in for the night. Realizing his mistake, he slammed the door shut and fled back into the gas.

At first, Yarrack thought some fool had simply stumbled into the old trap. Then he heard the shouting. His warriors began pulling on armor and gathering weapons while

Balok stumbled through the halls trying to stay ahead of the growing pursuit.

When he reached the main intersection again, his path was blocked. The orcs from the supply room and the guard room had gathered around the Boss who had uncovered the false alarm. They saw him emerge from the trapped corridor and charged.

Instead of fighting, Balok turned south. Ahead of him stood one last unopened door. Ignoring the warning signs carved upon it, he threw it open and found himself in Great Ulfe's own chamber.

The ogre chief was still asleep. His dire wolves were not. The beasts sprang to defend their master. Balok retreated immediately, slamming the heavy door behind him before the wolves could break free.

There was nowhere left to run.

With enemies behind him, enemies ahead of him, and the wolves pounding against the door at his back, Balok lowered his shoulder and charged into the assembled orcs. The fight was short. The Blooded Hand did not kill him.

When Balok awoke, he was bruised, battered, and still exhausted. His armor was gone. Shatterspike was gone. Every weapon, every tool, and every scrap of equipment had been stripped from him. He found himself locked inside the same crude cage he had discovered earlier that night. For the first time since entering Khundrukar, the half-orc had no weapon in his hand.

handouts.contentText:
I do not remember crawling into the cave.

I remember mud in my teeth. I remember reeds dragging across my face. I remember one hand on stone, then another, then nothing beneath me but cold ground and the smell of old smoke.

After that, memory broke apart.

Sometimes I was in the cave. Sometimes I was a boy again.

The roof above me became hide stretched over poles. The dripping water became rain on rag-wrapped furs. The stink of rot and swamp became the stink of a sickbed, old sweat, bad herbs, and my mother trying not to cough because she thought I was asleep.

I was not asleep.

I was never asleep when she coughed.

She used to turn her face away when it got bad. Like I would not hear the wetness in it. Like I would not see how thin her hands had become. She had been strong once. Stronger than most of the men who looked at her like she had done something shameful by keeping me alive. She had taught me where to stand when knives came out, how to watch eyes instead of hands, how to hear danger before it spoke.

Then sickness took the weight from her bones.

I saw her again in the cave. Not as she was at the end, but as she had been before we left the tribe. Broad-shouldered. Hard-eyed. Standing between me and those who spat when I passed.

Too human, they said.

Too soft in the face.

Too much of the wrong blood.

In the fever, I heard them again.

Orcs.

At first I thought they were ghosts from the old camp. Their voices came through the cave mouth in pieces, low and rough, speaking the tongue I learned before Common. My hand went looking for a weapon before my eyes opened.

Shatterspike was there.

I could not lift it.

That was when I knew how bad it was.

I lay in a hollow behind old stone and broken cult rubbish, tucked in darkness where the cave wall bent inward. I must have dragged myself there without knowing it. My armor was still on me, though loose in places where straps had torn or been cut. My body felt swollen inside the shell of it. Every breath hurt. My throat burned. I was thirsty enough to drink mud.

The voices came closer.

Blooded Hand.

Not the orcs from my childhood. Not my mother’s people. These were Ulfe’s dogs, and they were angry at being sent back to a dead cave.

One of them kicked something near the entrance. Bone, maybe. Or old wood. Another told him to stop making noise.

They were searching.

I closed my eyes and tried to slow my breathing.

My mother’s voice came back then, clear as a slap.

Do not move when hiding is all you have. Fear makes noise. Pain makes noise. Let them pass.

I let them pass.

Boots scraped stone. A torch hissed. The orange light reached across the cave floor but did not quite find me. I could see their shadows moving, huge and crooked against the walls. Three of them, maybe four. It was hard to count. The fever made one shadow into two, two into a crowd.

One of them said Great Ulfe was a fool for caring what dead dragon-men left behind.

Another told him to shut his mouth unless he wanted Ulfe to take his tongue.

That name kept me awake.

Ulfe.

I knew enough of the Blooded Hand to hate hearing it.

They overturned old bedding. Split rotten crates. Dug through ashes. One of them found a scrap of painted leather and cursed when it fell apart in his hand. Another said the cultists must have had orders, letters, maps, something. Great Ulfe said they missed something the first time. Great Ulfe wanted proof. Great Ulfe wanted names.

One of the orcs laughed at that.

“Names of who? We killed them.”

The answer came from another voice, older and meaner.

“Not them. The ones behind them.”

That quieted the cave.

I held still, but my mind did not. It slipped backward again, to another cave, another hiding place, another group of men looking for me.

Not orcs that time.

Humans.

Alley hounds. City rats with knives and boots and men behind them who sent boys to bleed for coin. I had stolen from them for the little vial I thought was medicine. I came back proud, lip split, knuckles open, holding it like treasure. My mother smelled it and knew at once it was not medicine. I saw it in her face, though she hid it fast.

She drank it anyway.

She told me I had done well.

In the cave, one of Ulfe’s orcs spat and said the dragon cult had more soldiers than Ulfe thought. Not a few robe-wearers in a swamp cave. Not just messengers. A host somewhere. A real host. Banners, riders, priests, beasts. The words were not clean in my head. They came broken between the fever and the torch smoke.

Army.

Dragon queen.

Revenge.

Ulfe had killed their emissaries. That much I understood. He had thought them small. Useful to rob. Easy to silence. Now he was afraid he had bitten something larger than his mouth.

Good.

Let him choke.

The thought almost made me smile, but even that hurt too much.

One of the searchers came nearer.

His boots stopped close enough that I could smell wet leather and old blood. He breathed through his mouth. I watched the edge of his shadow slide over the stone in front of me.

I wanted to move. My body begged me to move. To get a hand around Shatterspike. To rise. To make the cave red.

But I could not even trust my fingers.

So I hid.

There is no honor in dying because pride cannot stay quiet.

My mother taught me that too, though not in those words.

The orc turned away.

The light moved with him.

I breathed again only after I could no longer hear his boots.

They searched for a long while. Long enough that the torch burned low and the cave filled with greasy smoke. Long enough that I drifted again.

My mother woke me before dawn.

Go now, she said.

I told her no.

She struck me. Not hard. Hard enough.

Anger walks forward. Grief kneels.

I did not understand that then. I hated her for a little while. Not long. By the time I understood, she was dead, and I was already running south with a pack too light for the road and men hunting me for blood I did not know I had spilled.

The orcs were leaving when I came back to myself.

One of them said Ulfe would not like it.

Another said Ulfe could come dig through swamp filth himself.

The older one said they had found enough. Not papers, maybe, but signs. Marks. Bits of wax. Some scrap with a claw mark burned into it. Proof the cult had been taking orders from someone above the dead emissaries.

Then the voices faded into the rain.

I did not move for a long time.

Maybe hours.

Maybe until night.

Maybe until the next day.

When I finally crawled from the hollow, the cave was empty. The search had left everything worse than before. Old ashes scattered. Bones kicked aside. Rotten blankets torn open. The place stank of orc sweat and wet torch.

I found one scrap they missed.

Not much. A strip of stained hide with part of a symbol on it. A dragon’s wing, maybe. Or a claw. The fever made it swim when I looked at it too long.

I remembered words in pieces.

Ulfe afraid.

Cult army.

Emissaries dead.

Orders missing.

Revenge coming.

None of it settled right in my head. It was like trying to hold water in a broken cup. The more I reached for, the more I lost.

But I knew one thing.

The Blooded Hand was afraid of the dragon cult.

And if Ulfe was afraid, then there was something in the dark larger than orcs.

I kept the scrap.

Then I slept again.

When I woke the next time, I could sit up. Later, I could stand. Not well. Not for long. But enough.

Outside, the Black Mire waited.

Beyond it, the Stone Tooth.

Somewhere inside that mountain were my friends, or the bodies of my friends, or the ones who had killed them.

I tightened what straps remained on my armor. I checked the breathing mask. I took up Shatterspike.

My mother had told me once to sell my strength before I sold my fear.

I still had strength.

The fear could wait.

handouts.contentText:
By the time the others began to spit when Balok passed, she knew the camp was finished with them.

She had known from the moment he was born that he would never belong to her people for long. That had been the point of him, cruel as the truth was. She had taken a human warrior years before, not out of tenderness, not out of weakness, but because she had seen him fight and thought, there. There was strength that did not end in mud and smoke and old hatreds. There was blood that might make a child hard enough to survive the orcs and human enough to survive the world beyond them. For a few years she managed it. She fed him, hardened him, taught him what to watch for in the dark. But children grow into their faces, and Balok’s face gave him away. Too much human in the brow, the eyes, the shape of his mouth. The whispers became insults, the insults became hungers, and she understood before anyone said it plainly that if she stayed, the camp would kill him for being what she had made.

So she took him and left, pushing south toward the edges of Neverwinter with what little she could carry. They lived badly after that—ditch shelters, ruined huts, lean-tos in the reeds, any place where rain came through slower than the cold. Then sickness found her, the kind that does not roar but settles in the lungs like a patient beast. Balok watched her shrink by handfuls. Watched her cough until her ribs shook. She told him it was nothing. He did not believe her, but he was still young enough to think that if a thing had a cause, then surely it also had a cure. One morning, while she slept fitfully under rag-wrapped furs, he slipped into the city alone. He came back after dark with a split lip, stolen bruises, and a little stoppered vial clenched in both hands as if it were treasure. He had robbed the wrong men for it—alley hounds in service to harder bastards, the sort who answered insult with mutilation and debt with graves—and he stood over her, filthy and shaking and proud, telling her he had done it, that he had found medicine, that she only had to drink.

The moment she smelled it, she knew.

It was not medicine. It was some cheap gutter tonic, bitter spirits and herbs that dulled pain, perhaps, or sent fools to sleep, but nothing that would turn death aside. She saw, too, in the way his jaw was set and his knuckles were split, that he had paid dearly for it already. If she told him the truth, then the blows, the theft, the terror, all of it would become waste in his mind. Worse than waste. Failure. So she drank. She let the foulness burn down her throat and forced breath back into lungs that wanted none of it. Then she nodded once and told him, in the flat hard voice he trusted most, that he had done well. Balok sat beside her a long while after that, larger than a child already, still small enough to lean when he thought she would not notice. She put her hand on the back of his neck and left it there until he slept.

Before dawn she woke him and told him to go.

Not later. Not after she worsened. Not after the city came looking for what had been stolen. Go now, she said. South into Greenest - where his father had lived. Sell your strength before you sell your fear. Never stay where men call a chain protection. Never mistake being used for being wanted. He argued then, just once, and she struck him for it—not hard, but hard enough to make him angry instead of afraid, because anger walks forward and grief kneels. He left at sunrise with red eyes, a pack too light for any road, and the stubborn belief that he had bought her one more day. By the time the gang found her shelter, the boy was gone and she was already dead. But one of the men Balok had robbed had not survived the struggle, and that was more than they would bear unanswered. They found only a corpse, a stink of bad tonic, and no sign of the half-orc whelp who had slipped their hands. Men like that do not forgive humiliation, and they do not forget blood. So somewhere beneath all Balok’s later strength, all his caution, all his hard-earned talent for surviving under other men’s rules, there has always been this first lesson beating like a second heart: the world came hunting for him before he was even grown, and he has been running ever since.

handouts.title: The Night the False Sun Burned [Joric Burr]
handouts.summary:
I remember the sun painted on the orphanage door.

handouts.contentText:
I remember the sun painted on the orphanage door.

It was bright yellow then, cheerful as fresh bread, and meant to comfort those who passed beneath it. In Greenest, people believed that mark promised mercy. Many of the children who came to us had already been hollowed out by hunger, war, or grief before they ever crossed that threshold. Joric was one of them. I learned, in pieces, that his father had gone off to the orc wars and never returned, and that his mother—like too many women broken by waiting, poverty, and the slow cruelty of that time—left him behind when hope finally ran dry. By the time he came into church care, the world had already taught him that love could vanish, that men went to war and did not come home, and that children were often the first burden cast aside when survival grew thin.

I was young enough to believe the sunburst over our door meant safety too, still an acolyte, still foolish enough to think wickedness would always show its face plainly if only one looked hard enough. But evil had already learned to kneel, to pray, to wear the colors of Pelor and speak in gentle tones. I saw enough to know something was wrong long before I understood how deep the rot had gone. I saw children flinch at kindly voices. I saw bruises vanish beneath healing hands only to return by the next evening. I saw fear turned into routine. And because I was young, because I was afraid, because those above me wore the same holy symbols I did, I told myself I was powerless. That failure has lived with me longer than any scar.

One of those children was Joric.

He was small for his age, all sharp elbows and hungry eyes, forever hiding crusts in his sleeves and little scraps in his pockets as if the whole world had taught his hands not to trust tomorrow. He had a blunt tongue that earned him more cuffs than most, but even then there was something in him that refused to bow properly to cruelty. He would look at the priests with those hard young eyes of his, and I would think, with equal parts fear and shame, that this child had more courage than I did. The night Sir Braford came, it was Joric who found him. Not I, though I should have. Not any ordained soul in that place. A battered, frightened boy who still chose to speak.

I remember the sound before I remember the fire. Raised voices. Running feet. The crack of violence finally answered by violence in return. Sir Braford moved through that place like judgment given flesh, and for the first time the men who had hidden behind Pelor’s name found themselves facing someone who carried that name honestly. When the fighting ended, the church and the boarding house beside it burned. Some said the flames were only torchfire. Others said Pelor lent His wrath to cleanse what had been defiled. I have never cared which is true. I only know that I stood in that red light with ash on my face and understood, at last, that mercy without courage is only surrender dressed in holy language.

Now the Infirmary of Pelor stands where that place once stood. The walls are clean, the windows open wide, and the beds are for healing only. I have spent years tending the broken on that ground, and every kindness I offer feels, in some small way, like an unpaid debt. I do not know what became of Joric after those days. Perhaps he found peace. Perhaps he found anger. Perhaps he found a road that led him far from Greenest and every memory buried beneath these stones. But I have never forgotten his name. If he yet lives, he would be grown now, and I wonder whether I would know his face at once, while he might look straight through mine and see only another old sister in white and gold.

handouts.title: The Awakened Spellbook [Ezzilby Bibblesnitch]
handouts.summary: Instead, each tower received Ezzilby with the same careful politeness, the same measured voices and distant smiles. He would lay the book before them, small hands steady, and begin again—explaining how the ink shifted, how the scales did not weigh matter but meaning, how the structure corrected itself without formula.
handouts.contentText:
Instead, each tower received Ezzilby with the same careful politeness, the same measured voices and distant smiles. He would lay the book before them, small hands steady, and begin again—explaining how the ink shifted, how the scales did not weigh matter but meaning, how the structure corrected itself without formula. They would listen, nodding thoughtfully, offering soft interruptions like “yes, quite clever” or “an imaginative approach,” and when he finished, they would slide the book back toward him with gentle finality, remarking that it was “inconsistent,” “unreliable,” or simply “not how magic is properly done.”

He thanked them every time.

He adjusted his explanations, shortened them, simplified them, trying to meet them where they stood—but it never mattered. By the last tower, they barely opened the cover before returning it, one remarking that it was “a curiosity at best,” another adding, almost kindly, that “with proper training, you might yet produce something of value.” Ezzilby accepted the book as he always did, careful and composed, though his grip lingered a moment longer than before. He did not argue. He did not defend it. But as he stepped back into the street, something quiet and certain settled behind his eyes—if they could not see it, then it was never meant for them.

High above, behind doors that did not open for guests, the same men gathered in silence around scattered attempts to copy what they had dismissed. Ink bled across parchment in failed patterns, equations collapsing into nonsense no matter how they were arranged. One muttered that “it refuses structure,” another, more strained, admitted that “it works in his hands,” and a third, unable to hide the edge in his voice, whispered that “he has done something we cannot.” The room held that truth like a wound until, at last, the eldest spoke plainly: “We will not replicate it… we will take it.”

And far below, unaware—or perhaps simply unconcerned—Ezzilby Bibblesnitch walked on with the book tucked safely at his side, its shifting scales settling, just for a moment, into a balance no other mind had yet been able to grasp.

handouts.title: Mercy That Cost a Name [Loneoak]

handouts.contentText:
The summer the wells failed, the whole village learned how quiet grown folk could become. The fields had split open like old bread, the creek was all stones and flies, and even the dogs stopped barking by noon. My mother would send me with a bucket each morning anyway, as if hope might gather in it if I stared hard enough. We all did foolish things then. We prayed over empty cups. We scraped dampness from shaded rocks. We watched the elders lie with brave voices and cracked lips, saying the clouds were only late.

I saw him on the fourth morning past the last full jug. I had gone farther than I was meant to, up where the thornbrush leaned over the path and the heat shimmered so hard it made the trees look like ghosts. He stood between the pines, taller than any man I had ever seen, broad-shouldered and heavy with the stillness of an old tree. His face was hidden at first by shadow and a wide traveler's hat, but I remember the blue of him most of all: blue fur around his cheeks and throat like a wild mane, blue skin at the hands, and a strange calm to him that made the woods seem to hold their breath. Great hornlike antlers rose from his head, and his leathers were layered with travel straps, pouches, weathered armor, and little charms that clicked softly when he moved. In one hand he carried a crooked staff wrapped with roots and dangling things I did not know. He looked like no priest from any shrine, no forester from any lord's road. He looked like the deep woods had decided to walk.

He held one hand over the dry run of the streambed, and though I heard no chant, no thunder, no prayer, the stones beneath him darkened. Water gathered there in clear trembling ribbons, then in a rush, then in a running thread bright enough to make me cry out. He turned at the sound. Then I saw his face beneath the brim: stern, tired, and kind in a way that hurt to look at. Not soft—never soft—but burdened, as if mercy had weight and he had chosen to carry it. He lifted one finger to his lips, not sternly, but gently, like a secret shared instead of commanded. Then he stepped back into the trees. I think the leaves bent around him to hide him. By the time I ran to the stream and dropped to my knees, gulping water with both hands, he was gone. When I looked up again, there was only the wind in the branches and the feeling that someone had given us something he would suffer for.

The village said the spring had returned. The priest said the gods had heard us. My mother said not every mercy needs a name. I kept mine for him anyway. In my thoughts I called him the Blue Giant, the Horned One, the Quiet Keeper of Rain. Years later, when travelers spoke of hidden grove-folk and druids who guarded the wild with laws older than kings, I wondered if one of them had broken faith for us. If that is true, then somewhere there walks an exile who chose thirsty children over ancient law. I was only small when I saw him, but I have never forgotten this: the world was dying, and he gave it water with the grief of a man who knew the cost before he paid it.
